story:
Since our trip to British Columbia in 2022, I had known I wanted to return with Tyler. I decided we would take the same approach as before: leave early and take our time winding through Banff, Lake Louise, Jasper, and the rest of the Canadian Rockies. The drive was seventeen hours in total, stretched comfortably over three days, and it was extraordinary. Sharing the road with Tyler and my dad, watching the scenery unfold and meeting the occasional character along the way, made the journey its own reward.

One of the strongest reasons I wanted to go back was the family we hunt with. Dan and Ellen Brooks have a gift for making you feel at home the moment you arrive. Ellen’s home-cooked meals are legendary, and Dan is a born storyteller. This year Dan had another family in camp as well, which meant we would get the chance to hunt with Cody again.

The goal was clear: Dad and I wanted to take bears with our bows, and Tyler needed his first. The first evening we began seeing some truly impressive animals. Knowing what the country can produce, we made a point of keeping Tyler off the trigger so he wouldn’t settle for the first bear that stepped out.

On Tuesday, Cody took us onto private ground where bears had been getting aggressive with the livestock. We had glassed a couple of big boars there that morning, so we circled back in the evening. In the far corner of the field where we had seen a large boar earlier, a bear finally stepped into the open. Excitement took over. We had a long stretch of open ground to cover with no cover of our own, so I sent Tyler ahead with Cody and made it clear I didn’t want him shooting unless it was a big bear.

A moment later Cody had Tyler settled over the sticks. A single shot cracked. I couldn’t see the bear—only heard the solid hit. Tyler’s face told me everything. When we reached the animal we discovered it was a smaller sow. For the ranch it was perfect; sows can be especially aggressive around calves during calving season. For Tyler’s first bear, it wasn’t what I had envisioned. Cody realized almost immediately that it wasn’t the bear we thought we were looking at. We decided to get Tyler another tag and chalk the first one up to conservation.

One comic moment came while we were bringing the truck down to the field edge to load the bear. Cody never saw the big hole in the ground. We hit it at thirty or forty miles an hour and everything went airborne. Tyler still tells the best version of that story. I won’t lie—it hurt.

Wednesday became a reset day. We had picked up a flat the evening before, so we started at the tire shop, got it fixed, and put the spare back on. We should have been good to go. We weren’t. While checking some remote roads we heard a strange sound from the rear of the truck. Suddenly the tire itself came flying past my window and we lurched to a stop. With no cell service, I managed to get a message out on the Garmin to Ellen. She sent one of the girls with another truck. It would be two full days before a tow truck could pull Cody’s rig out of the mountains and get it repaired. We’re fairly certain the lug nuts simply hadn’t been torqued properly. Two days, two wild truck incidents.

Around midday a nice boar crossed the road. It was Dad’s turn. I set up with the spotting scope, intending to film, while Dad and Cody began the stalk. They closed to sixty yards. (I later discovered I had been taking still photos the entire time instead of recording video.) Dad made a clean archery shot. One more bear down, and I couldn’t have been happier watching my father take one with a bow—a little redemption after a couple of chaotic days.

Two bears down, two tags left. Thursday simply wasn’t our day. I had several chances to close the distance with my bow on different bears, but nothing quite came together. Failure after failure. A full day of hunting with nothing to show for it.

Friday—the last day. It was time to put the bow away and get a bear on the ground. The other family had left Thursday morning, so we split up. Tyler and Dad headed out with Dan while Cody and I went looking for the animal we had started calling the “bingo bear”—a big chocolate that would appear for a moment and vanish just as quickly.

We were down to the final couple of hours and still hadn’t found the one we wanted. While checking a new stretch of country we came around a bend and found Dan’s truck parked on the shoulder. Tyler was waving us down. He had just killed a stud of a bear minutes before we arrived. The timing could not have been better. I got to see that huge smile on his face and squeeze into a photo with him. It was perfect.

Then it was straight back to hunting, and time was running short. In the last hour of evening light we circled back to a spot where we had seen a good bear earlier. I glanced right, then left toward Cody. His eyes were wide and he was already smiling as we rolled to a stop. I didn’t know exactly what was about to happen, but I was all in.

We piled out, grabbed the rifle, dropped into the borrow pit, and slipped forward twenty yards until we could see into the clearing. A hundred yards away stood the bingo bear. I settled over the sticks and squeezed the trigger.

Tag notched.

We finished the trip with four bears and a lifetime of memories. British Columbia has become a special place for our family.
